analysis.body:
The Census BTOS measure, first asked in September 2023, puts AI use at 41.0% for finance and insurance firms (NAICS 52) answering yes to using AI in the last two weeks. The prior period figure was 36.5%. This figure covers finance and insurance together rather than insurance alone.

Per NAIC, AI in insurance is deployed across underwriting, pricing, customer service, claims handling, marketing, and fraud detection. Some insurers use AI powered chatbots to answer common customer questions and assist with simple transactions at any time. In claims processing, AI can help estimate repair costs or assess damage using photos and historical data. NAIC also notes a shift from detect and repair toward predict and prevent, with AI identifying risks earlier and helping customers avoid losses.

NAIC describes the supervisory frame. State insurance regulators oversee insurers' use of AI and may require companies to explain how tools are used in underwriting, pricing, marketing, or claims decisions. Insurers remain responsible for complying with insurance laws, regulations, standards, and consumer protection rules, including fairness, accuracy, and avoiding unfair discrimination. Human oversight remains an important part of insurance decision making. The NAIC model bulletin on insurers' use of AI, adopted by a growing majority of states, is the operative US governance document for the sector. NAIC began surveying insurers by line of business in 2021, with aggregate reports on private passenger auto, homeowners, life, and health issued in December 2022, August 2023, December 2023, and May 2025.

External evaluators also track the sector. AM Best evaluates innovation and digital maturity as part of its assessments, with technology capability reaching credit opinion. The Evident AI Index benchmarks major global insurers on AI talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency, serving as the sector's comparative maturity scoreboard.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material shows adoption is measurable and rising, but the regulatory layer is active. NAIC warns that large language models do not truly understand context and may generate information that sounds accurate but is incorrect, so AI generated information should be reviewed carefully, especially for important decisions. AI is more likely to support human workers than replace them entirely, and insurers using AI still answer to state regulators for fairness and accuracy.

https://content.naic.org/.brief: The homepage invites users to explore recent publications, the latest news articles, new federal and legislative news, and model laws. It presents these resources as a way to help inform their approach. The page is organized to provide quick access to up-to-date regulatory information. Users can browse the listed materials to stay current with relevant laws and guidance.

https://content.naic.org/insurance-topic.brief: NAIC created the Innovation Cybersecurity and Technology Committee in 2021 to discuss how new technology, including AI, affects insurance regulation. The Big Data and Artificial Intelligence Working Group, established in 2019, produced regulatory principles on AI that NAIC members adopted in 2020, and has been surveying insurers across lines of business, issuing reports in December 2022, August 2023, December 2023, and May 2025. AI is applied in underwriting, pricing, customer service, claims handling, marketing, and fraud detection, and can help insurers shift from a “detect and repair” approach to a “predict and prevent” strategy. The Working Group notes that while AI can automate many tasks, human oversight remains essential for compliance with fairness, accuracy, and consumer protection rules.
